questions.question: What is the distribution of the minimum of independent exponentials with rates $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$?
options: Normal with mean equal to the largest rate
Uniform on the interval of rates
Exponential with rate $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_n$
Degenerate at the smallest rate

questions.question: What does the minimum represent in the clock interpretation?
options: The last clock to ring
The first waiting time among the clocks.
The average of all clock times
The rate of one selected clock only.

questions.question: What happens as more independent exponential clocks are running?
options: The first one tends to ring slower
The first time becomes deterministic
The first one tends to ring faster
The total rate becomes negative

questions.question: What is the probability that a particular clock is first?
options: Its rate multiplied by all other rates
Its rate divided by the total rate
The reciprocal of its rate only
Always $1/2$

questions.question: What assumption is required of the exponential random variables?
options: They are all deterministic
They are all uniform
They are independent
They have negative rates

questions.question: If two independent exponential times have rates $2$ and $3$, what is the rate of their minimum?
Two repair teams respond independently. What can model the first response time?
options: The maximum of two deterministic times only
A hypergeometric count
A sample median of all customers
The minimum of two exponential response times

questions.question: In competing failure modes with rates $0.1$ and $0.4$, what is the first-failure rate?
If buses from two routes arrive independently, what is the next bus time?
options: The maximum of the two waiting times
The minimum of the two route waiting times
The sum of both waiting times
The variance of both waiting times

questions.question: With rates $2$ and $3$, what is the probability the rate-$3$ clock is first?
Why does the minimum have a larger rate than each individual clock?
options: Any one of the clocks can produce the first event
The minimum waits for all clocks to ring
Rates are averaged rather than summed
Independence makes rates vanish

questions.question: How does this result connect to competing risks?
options: Each risk is an exponential clock; the earliest fires.
Competing risks must be sampled without replacement.
Only the slowest risk matters
All risks must have equal probability

questions.question: Why is independence important in the exponential race theorem?
options: The simple sum-of-rates formula relies on independent clocks
Dependence always makes the minimum deterministic
Independence is only needed for notation
Dependent clocks cannot have minima

questions.question: If rates are $1,4,5$, what is the distribution of the minimum?
options: $\operatorname{Exp}(5)$
$\operatorname{Exp}(10)$
$\operatorname{Pois}(10)$

questions.question: If rates are $1,4,5$, what is the probability the rate-$4$ clock is first?
Three independent repair teams have rates $2,2,6$. What is the mean first response time?
Why is the minimum an order statistic?
options: The first value after sorting the waiting times.
It is the average of the waiting times.
It is the last value after sorting
It is the probability of a route

questions.question: What misconception arises if rates are averaged instead of summed?
options: It understates the first event's speed among several clocks.
It gives exactly the theorem's result
It makes the fastest clock impossible
It changes exponentials into uniform variables.

questions.question: If one clock has rate $0$, why does it not affect the total race rate?
options: It makes the total rate zero
It contributes no arrivals to the sum of rates
It must win with probability one
It invalidates all positive-rate clocks

questions.question: A solution says the slowest exponential clock determines the minimum. What is wrong?
options: The minimum is always the largest observation.
Exponential clocks cannot be independent
Rates cannot be compared
The minimum is the first clock to ring, not the slowest.
